text: We've covered when to fine-tune, how to actually do it, and how to evaluate whether it worked. This last lesson in the chapter covers the question that usually gets answered too late: what does all of this actually cost, start to finish?

Five real cost components, and most teams only budget for one of them. Data collection — hundreds of good labeled examples, almost always the single largest cost, and it never shows up on a pricing page. Training compute, billed on tokens actually consumed. The inference surcharge, which is usually more per call, not less. Storage — a full fine-tune versus a tiny LoRA adapter. And re-tuning: a recurring cost that hits every single time the base model gets deprecated.

Training is billed on trained_tokens — the actual tokens your run consumed. Third-party pricing trackers have cited figures roughly between a dollar fifty and twenty-five dollars per million training tokens, varying a lot by model size. Treat any specific number here as approximate — confirm current pricing directly before you budget around it, because these rates move.

Here's the one that catches teams off guard: calling a fine-tuned model is typically more expensive per token than calling the base model it came from, not less. Pricing trackers have cited roughly one and a half times the base rate on some providers. If your fine-tuned model replaces millions of calls, that surcharge compounds fast — run the math on your real call volume before assuming fine-tuning saves money long term.

Stack it up against prompting, and the picture gets clearer. Prompting costs essentially nothing to set up, you pay only per call, and you never have to retrain. Fine-tuning stacks data cost, training cost, a higher ongoing inference rate, storage, and a re-tune every time the base model gets deprecated. That's a wider, more recurring cost picture than a single training bill suggests.

Data, training, inference, storage, and recurring re-tuning — that's the real cost of fine-tuning, and it's exactly why Lesson 20 said prompt first. That's Chapter 4 complete. Chapter 5 moves past text entirely — image generation, vision-language models, and audio, and when you actually need them instead of a text-only model. See you there.
